tldr: Tencent's Q3 capex jumped to RMB81.4bn against about RMB55bn expected, which pushed it into RMB13.7bn of net debt as revenue missed at RMB207bn. On the call, management warned that compute limits may delay the next Hunyuan model.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its $70-$78 range, ahead of its Nasdaq debut as ANT on Nov 19, per Bloomberg, CNBC and Reuters sources. Google launched Gemini 4 Neon at $3/$15 per million tokens and says it ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis' Coding Agent Index.

Nvidia said it has stopped shipping licensed Hopper chips to China after $2.4B of Q3 sales. The WSJ reports an SEC probe into its disclosures, and the stock gave up its earnings pop to close about 2.9% lower.

Capex hit RMB81.43bn against about RMB55.4bn expected, driven by large compute prepayments for Hunyuan upgrades, WorkBuddy inference and cloud customers. items.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, a $3/$15 coding and agent model it says tops Artificial Analysis' Coding Agent Index
items.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon on Nov 18. It sits between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon and targets multi-file software engineering, knowledge work and science, either alone or orchestrating Hydrogen subagents. It costs $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 cached) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1,048,576-token context window. Google says it scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at xhigh effort (#3 overall), 58.6 on the AA Coding Agent Index (#1) and 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, at 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It is rolling out in the Gemini API/AI Studio, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Antigravity and the Gemini app for Pro/Ultra users.
items.why_it_matters: This is Google's fourth new Gemini model in about a month, and it lands in the mid-price coding tier a day after OpenAI's GPT-6.2 and Microsoft's MAI Code 2, undercutting Carbon on cost per task.

items.title: Hugging Face shows a 180B-parameter MoE running in Transformers on 32GB of RAM by streaming experts from disk
items.summary: A Hugging Face blog post published Nov 18 ('180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers') describes running a 180B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a 32GB-RAM machine by loading expert weights from disk on demand. Technical takeaway: in a sparse MoE only a few experts fire per token, so keeping shared weights resident and paging in the active experts makes models far larger than RAM usable, at a throughput cost.
items.why_it_matters: It brings SSD expert streaming into the mainstream Transformers library, lowering the hardware needed to run large open MoEs locally.

learn.title: Check whether a one-point benchmark gap is signal or noise
learn.why_today: Google reports Gemini 4 Neon at 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, and search snippets say Claude Opus 5.5 scores slightly higher. Before reading a ranking into that, it helps to know how many tasks it takes to separate two pass rates.
learn.explanation: A pass rate on n tasks is a binomial proportion, so its standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n). That is about 5 points at n=89 and still about 1.5 points at n=1000. When two models run the same tasks, the gap's variance is reduced by the per-task correlation rho of their outcomes, because both tend to solve the same easy tasks. That is why paired comparisons are tighter than comparing two separate confidence intervals. Even so, resolving a 1.3-point gap at z=2 needs thousands of tasks unless rho is very high. Agentic benchmarks add run-to-run variance from sampling and the harness, so multiple seeds per task matter too. The Wilson interval is better than the normal approximation when p is near 0 or 1 or n is small.
learn.python:
import math
# Is a benchmark gap real? Illustrative pass rates, not any vendor's actual per-task data.
def wilson(p, n, z=1.96):
    c = p + z*z/(2*n); h = z*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z*z/(4*n*n)); d = 1 + z*z/n
    return (c - h)/d, (c + h)/d
def gap_se(pa, pb, n, rho):
    # SE of pa - pb when both models run the SAME n tasks; rho = per-task outcome correlation
    va, vb = pa*(1-pa)/n, pb*(1-pb)/n
    return math.sqrt(va + vb - 2*rho*math.sqrt(va*vb))
pa, pb = 0.652, 0.665   # model A vs model B: a 1.3-point gap
for n in (89, 300, 1000):
    lo, hi = wilson(pa, n)
    print(f"n={n:5d}  A 95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]", end="")
    for rho in (0.0, 0.6):
        z = (pb - pa)/gap_se(pa, pb, n, rho)
        print(f"  rho={rho}: z={z:.2f}", end="")
    print()
# tasks needed to resolve a 1.3-pt gap at z=2 with paired rho=0.6
se_needed = (pb - pa)/2
v = pa*(1-pa) + pb*(1-pb) - 2*0.6*math.sqrt(pa*(1-pa)*pb*(1-pb))
print("tasks needed:", math.ceil(v/se_needed**2))

learn.title: Estimate MoE decode speed when experts are streamed from SSD
learn.why_today: Hugging Face describes running a 180B-parameter MoE in Transformers on 32GB of RAM by loading experts from disk, so it is worth knowing what limits the speed of that approach.
learn.explanation: In a top-k MoE each token touches k of E experts per layer, so per-token weight traffic is about L*k*bytes_per_expert, not the full model. If experts live on SSD, decode speed is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes missed per token, so an expert cache in RAM helps in proportion to its hit rate. Under uniform routing the hit rate is just cache/E, which makes small caches nearly useless. Real routers are skewed and consecutive tokens reuse experts, so measured hit rates are higher, and that skew is what makes streaming practical. Prefetching the next layer's experts while the current one computes can hide part of the latency, but not the bandwidth. The numbers below are illustrative and do not describe the model in the post.
learn.python:
# Expert streaming: how fast can a MoE decode when experts live on SSD? Illustrative config, not a real model.
L, E, k = 60, 128, 8           # layers, experts per layer, experts active per token
expert_bytes = 11e6            # one expert at 4-bit: 60*128*11MB ~ 84 GB ~ 170B params (illustrative)
ssd_bw = 6e9                   # NVMe read bandwidth, bytes/s
for cache_per_layer in (0, 8, 16, 32):
    # assume uniform routing: P(an active expert is already cached) = cache/E
    miss = 1 - cache_per_layer/E
    bytes_per_token = L * k * miss * expert_bytes
    tps = ssd_bw / bytes_per_token
    ram_gb = L * cache_per_layer * expert_bytes / 1e9
    print(f"cache {cache_per_layer:3d}/layer  RAM for experts {ram_gb:5.1f} GB  "
          f"read {bytes_per_token/1e9:5.2f} GB/token  ~{tps:5.2f} tok/s")
print("total expert weights:", round(L*E*expert_bytes/1e9, 1), "GB")
